beats.say: Siya buys 11 stickers, and each one costs 25 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 11 stickers costs 25 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 11 and 25 would mix up stickers and rupees. We need 11 lots of 25 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 11 lots of 25. That is a times sum.
11 is 10 and 1. So work out 10 lots first, then 1 more lot.
10 lots of 25 is 250. And 1 more lot is just 25.
Add the two parts. 250 and 25 make 275.
So the total cost is 275 rupees.
Does that make sense? 11 stickers must cost a lot more than one, and 275 is a lot more than 25. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Siddharth buys 12 erasers, and each one costs 15 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 12 erasers costs 15 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 12 and 15 would mix up erasers and rupees. We need 12 lots of 15 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 12 lots of 15. That is a times sum.
12 is 10 and 2. So work out 10 lots first, then the other 2 lots.
10 lots of 15 is 150. And 2 times 15 is 30.
Add the two parts. 150 and 30 make 180.
So the total cost is 180 rupees.
Does that make sense? 12 erasers must cost a lot more than one, and 180 is a lot more than 15. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Isha buys 10 pens, and each one costs 10 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 10 pens costs 10 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 10 and 10 would mix up pens and rupees. We need 10 lots of 10 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 10 lots of 10. That is a times sum.
10 times 10 is 100. So the total cost is 100 rupees.
Does that make sense? 10 pens must cost a lot more than one, and 100 is a lot more than 10. Yes.
So when every item costs the same, the total is the number of items times the price of one.
Neha pays 60 rupees for the book, then sells it at a profit of 10 percent. We want the selling price.
Percent means out of every 100. 10 out of 100 is one tenth. So 10 percent of a number is the number divided by 10.
60 divided by 10 is 6. So the profit is 6 rupees.
Now, the selling price. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: A profit means Neha gets more money back than was paid. So the 6 is added to the cost.

beats.say: A profit means selling for more than the cost. So add the profit to the cost.
60 plus 6 is 66. So the selling price is 66 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 6 is only the profit. The question asks for the selling price, which is 66.
So find the profit first, then add it to the cost.
Three signs in one sum: a divide, a plus and a times. The trick is knowing where to start.
One of these three signs has to wait until the very end. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times both go before plus. So the plus is the one that waits until the end.

beats.say: Dividing and multiplying go before adding. So we box 20 divided by 2, and we box 4 times 2.
First box. 20 divided by 2 is 10, because 2 times 10 is 20.
Second box. 4 times 2 is 8.
Put each answer where its box was, with the plus still in between.
Now the plus gets its turn. 10 plus 8 is 18.
Careful with the trap. Do not add in the middle first. The plus joins the two boxes, so it comes last.
The rule: do the dividing and the multiplying first. The adding comes last.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus, even though the plus is written first. So we begin with 6 times 7.

beats.say: Times goes before plus, so put a box round 6 times 7.
6 times 7 is 42. So 42 goes where the box was, and the rest stays the same.
One job left, the adding. 43 and 42 make 85.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 43 and 6 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 6 belongs to the times.
So remember: times first, then the plus.
Look at the signs here. A minus, then a times, then a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 4 times 7.

beats.say: Times is the boss here. It goes before plus and minus, so put a box round 4 times 7.
4 times 7 is 28. Write 28 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 44 take away 28.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 44 take away 28 is 16.
And now the plus. 16 plus 2 is 18.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a minus.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 27 times 2 is our first job. The 15 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
27 times 2. 20 times 2 is 40, and 7 times 2 is 14. Together that makes 54.
So 54 goes where the box was. The minus 15 is still there.
Now the minus. 54 take away 15 is 39.
Careful with one thing. The 15 is not part of the times. It is only taken away after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
Look at the signs here. A minus, then a times, then a plus.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 3 times 5.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 3 times 5. It goes first.
3 times 5 is 15. Write 15 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 63 take away 15.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 63 take away 15 is 48.
One job left, the plus. 48 and 1 make 49.
The trap in this sum is the minus at the front. It looks like the place to start, but the times must go first.
The rule: multiply first. Then add and take away in order, from left to right.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a plus.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 7 times 7 is our first job. The 4 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
7 times 7 is 49.
So 49 goes where the box was. The plus 4 is still there.
Now the plus. 49 plus 4 is 53.
Careful with one thing. The 4 is not part of the times. It is only added on after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a plus.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 22 times 9 is our first job. The 10 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
22 times 9. 20 times 9 is 180, and 2 times 9 is 18. Together that makes 198.
So 198 goes where the box was. The plus 10 is still there.
Now the plus. 198 plus 10 is 208.
Careful with one thing. The 10 is not part of the times. It is only added on after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes before adding, so 8 times 2 is our first job.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding. So we box the 8 times 2. It goes first.
8 times 2 is 16. Write 16 in its place, and copy the rest just as it was.
One job left, the adding. 41 and 16 make 57.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 41 and 8 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 8 belongs to the times.
The rule: multiply before you add, wherever the times sign sits.
Rohan buys 8 books, and each one costs 3 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 8 books costs 3 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 8 and 3 would mix up books and rupees. We need 8 lots of 3 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 8 lots of 3. That is a times sum.
8 times 3 is 24. So the total cost is 24 rupees.
Does that make sense? 8 books must cost a lot more than one, and 24 is a lot more than 3. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Karan buys 4 stickers, and each one costs 15 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 4 stickers costs 15 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 4 and 15 would mix up stickers and rupees. We need 4 lots of 15 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 4 lots of 15. That is a times sum.
4 times 15. 4 times 10 is 40, and 4 times 5 is 20. Together that makes 60.
So the total cost is 60 rupees.
Does that make sense? 4 stickers must cost a lot more than one, and 60 is a lot more than 15. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Riya pays 500 rupees for the bicycle, then sells it at a loss of 25 percent. We want the selling price.
Percent means out of every 100. 25 out of 100 is one quarter. To find a quarter, halve the number, then halve it again.
Half of 500 is 250. Half of 250 is 125. So the loss is 125 rupees.
Now, the selling price. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: A loss means Riya gets less money back than was paid. So the 125 is taken away from the cost.

beats.say: A loss means selling for less than the cost. So take the loss away from the cost.
500 take away 125 is 375. So the selling price is 375 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 125 is only the loss. The question asks for the selling price, which is 375.
So find the loss first, then take it away from the cost.
Here is our sum. It has two parts with a minus in between. The two parts look almost the same, but they are not.
Take the first part. It has a little bracket inside it. What do we do first there?

ask.ifNot: A bracket always goes first. So inside the first part we begin with 2 plus 3.

beats.say: Brackets first. 2 plus 3 is 5. Then 5 times 5 is 25. So the first part is 25.
Now the second part. Careful, here is the trap. This time there is no little bracket round the 2 plus 3.
So which goes first in the second part?

ask.ifNot: With no bracket to say otherwise, times goes before plus. So 3 times 5 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. Then 2 plus 15 is 17. So the second part is 17.
Now take the second part away from the first. 25 take away 17 is 8.
See what the little bracket did? With it we got 25. Without it we got 17. Same numbers, different order.
So remember: brackets first, then times, then plus and minus.
Here is our sum. It has a minus, a times, a plus and a divide, all in one line. Where do we start?
Which two jobs go first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide always go before plus and minus. So 2 times 3, and 15 divided by 3, go first.

beats.say: Times and divide go before plus and minus. So we box them both.
2 times 3 is 6. And 15 divided by 3 is 5.
Put each answer where its box was. Now the sum is 13 minus 6 plus 5.
Only a minus and a plus are left. Which one first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go left to right, like reading. 13 take away 6 comes first.

beats.say: 13 take away 6 is 7. Then 7 plus 5 is 12.
Watch out for one slip. The 3 and the 15 sit side by side, but we must not add them. Each one belongs to its own box.
So: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here are two sums with an empty box between them. We work out each side, then decide which sign fits in the box.
Left side first: 2 plus 3 times 2. There is no bracket here. So which goes first?

ask.ifNot: With no bracket, times goes before plus. So 3 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6, and 2 plus 6 is 8. The left side is 8.
Now the right side. This one has a bracket, and a bracket always goes first. 3 plus 2 is 5.
Then 2 times 5 is 10. The right side is 10.
So we compare 8 with 10. Which is true?

ask.ifNot: 8 is smaller than 10. The sign opens wide towards the bigger number, so its small pointed end faces the 8.

beats.say: 8 is less than 10. So the sign in the box is the less than sign.
Did you see the trap? Both sides use the same numbers. But the bracket changes the order, so the two answers are different.
So work out each side on its own, following the order rules, and only then compare.
Raunak buys 12 dozen and Shail buys 5 score. To compare them, we first turn both into plain numbers.
A dozen is 12. Do you know how many a score is?

ask.ifNot: A score is an old word for 20. So 5 score means 5 lots of 20.

beats.say: One dozen is 12, and one score is 20. Let us write that down.
Raunak has 12 dozen. That is 12 times 12. 10 twelves are 120, and 2 twelves are 24. Together, 144.
Shail has 5 score. 5 times 20 is 100.
144 is more than 100, so Raunak has more. How do we find how many more?

ask.ifNot: How many more means the gap between the two numbers. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: 144 take away 100 is 44. So Raunak has 44 more.
Careful with one thing. We cannot just compare the 12 and the 5. A dozen and a score are different sizes, so change both into numbers first.
So: turn both into plain numbers, then subtract to find the gap.
Here is our sum, with four signs in a row: plus, times, minus and divide. The order we do them in matters.
Which jobs must be done before any adding or taking away?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide go before plus and minus. So 9 times 3, and 8 divided by 2, come first.

beats.say: So we box 9 times 3, and we box 8 divided by 2.
9 times 3 is 27. And 8 divided by 2 is 4.
Now write the sum again, with 27 and 4 where the boxes were.
Only a plus and a minus are left, so we go left to right. 7 plus 27 is 34.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: Look at the sum again. There is still a minus 4 at the end, waiting for its turn.

beats.say: One job is still waiting. 34 take away 4 is 30.
So: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right, all the way to the end.
Three empty boxes, and each one needs a sign. The finished sum must equal 20. We test the choices one at a time.
Try plus, times, divide. Times and divide go first. 3 times 7 is 21, then 21 divided by 6. That does not share out evenly, so cross it off.
Next try minus, times, plus. 3 times 7 is 21 again. But we cannot take 21 away from 5, so this one is out too.
Now try plus, times, minus. Which bit do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 3 times 7 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 7 is 21. So the sum becomes 5 plus 21 minus 6.
Left to right now. 5 plus 21 is 26, and 26 take away 6 is 20. That is the number we wanted!
So the signs are plus, times, minus.
When you test signs like this, always follow the order rules: times and divide before plus and minus.
This sum says the answer is 41. As it stands, that is not what we get. Our job is to put in one bracket that makes it true.
First see why it needs help. With no bracket, times goes first, and 8 times 4 is 32. But we cannot take 32 away from 17.
A bracket says: do me first. Which bracket would stop the 8 times 4 from going first?

ask.ifNot: A bracket round 8 times 4 changes nothing, because times goes first anyway. We need the taking away to go first, so bracket 17 minus 8.

beats.say: Try it. Put the bracket round 17 minus 8.
Bracket first. 17 take away 8 is 9.
Then the times. 9 times 4 is 36.
Then the plus. 36 plus 5 is 41. That is exactly the number we wanted!
So the bracket goes round 17 minus 8.
The other brackets leave us taking a big number away from 17, so they cannot work. The key idea: a bracket moves a job to the front of the queue.
Half a dozen bananas cost 30 rupees. We want to know how many bananas 85 rupees will buy.

board.text: Half a dozen bananas cost 30 rupees

beats.say: First, how many bananas is half a dozen?

ask.ifNot: A dozen is 12, and half of 12 is 6. So half a dozen is 6 bananas.

beats.say: A dozen is 12, so half a dozen is 6. That means 6 bananas cost 30 rupees.
Now find the price of one banana. Share 30 rupees among 6 bananas. 30 divided by 6 is 5.
So one banana costs 5 rupees. How do we find how many bananas 85 rupees buys?

ask.ifNot: Each banana uses up 5 rupees. So we count how many fives there are in 85. That is 85 divided by 5.

beats.say: 85 divided by 5. Split 85 into 50 and 35. 50 is 10 fives, and 35 is 7 fives.
10 fives and 7 fives make 17 fives. So 85 rupees buys 17 bananas.
Check by multiplying back. 17 bananas at 5 rupees each cost 85 rupees. It fits.
So: find the price of one first. Then divide the money by that price.
We must find the one statement that is completely true. So we test each one in turn. No guessing.
First: is 240 divided by 16 more than 16? Think in times. 16 times 10 is 160, and 16 times 5 is 80. Together, 240.
So 240 divided by 16 is 15. And 15 is less than 16, not more. This one is not true.
Second: is 18 plus 18 divided by 2 equal to 18? Which bit goes first here?

ask.ifNot: Divide goes before plus. So 18 divided by 2 comes first.

beats.say: 18 divided by 2 is 9, and 18 plus 9 is 27, not 18. So this one is not true either.
Now the long one. Left side first. 17 times 10 is 170, and 17 times 7 is 119. So 17 times 17 is 289.
Add the 18. 289 plus 18 is 307. So the left side is 307.
Right side. 16 times 16 is 256, and 17 times 3 is 51.
256 plus 51 is 307. The right side is 307 too!
Both sides are 307, so this statement is the true one.
The trap: a statement can look right at a glance. Work out both sides fully before you believe it.
A mystery number, divided by 8, gives 12 with nothing left over. Then the same number is divided by 3. What do we get?
First we must find the mystery number. How?

ask.ifNot: Dividing by 8 gave 12. To go back, we do the opposite of dividing, which is multiplying. 8 times 12.

beats.say: Times undoes divide. So the number is 8 times 12. 8 times 10 is 80, and 8 times 2 is 16. Together, 96.
The mystery number is 96. Now we divide 96 by 3.
Split 96 into 90 and 6. 90 divided by 3 is 30, and 6 divided by 3 is 2.
30 and 2 make 32. So the new quotient, the answer to the division, is 32.
Check by multiplying back. 3 times 32 is 96. It fits.
Careful with the trap. Do not just mix up the 8, the 12 and the 3. Find the mystery number first, and then divide it.
One gross of notebooks costs 2592 rupees. We need the cost of 68 notebooks.
A gross is 12 dozen. How many notebooks is that?

ask.ifNot: 12 dozen is 12 lots of 12. And 12 times 12 is 144.

beats.say: 12 dozen is 12 times 12, which is 144. So 144 notebooks cost 2592 rupees.
Next we want the cost of one notebook. That is 2592 divided by 144. Think in times: 144 times what makes 2592?
Try 20, because it is easy. 144 times 2 is 288, so 144 times 20 is 2880. That is too big.
How much too big? 2880 take away 2592 is 288. And 288 is exactly 2 lots of 144. So we need 2 lots fewer than 20.
20 take away 2 is 18. So one notebook costs 18 rupees.
Now, 68 notebooks at 18 rupees each. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 68 notebooks costs 18 rupees. So we need 68 lots of 18.

beats.say: Use the same trick. 18 is 20 take away 2. 68 times 2 is 136, so 68 times 20 is 1360.
That is 2 lots of 68 too many, so take away 136. 1360 take away 136 is 1224.
So 68 notebooks cost 1224 rupees.
The key idea: do not jump straight from a gross to 68. Find the cost of one notebook first, then multiply.
This looks scary, but it is only brackets inside brackets. The rule: start at the innermost bracket and work outwards.
Which bracket is the innermost one?

ask.ifNot: The round bracket sits inside the square one. So the round bracket, 35 minus 2 times 12, goes first.

beats.say: Inside the round bracket there is a minus and a times. Careful: times goes first. 2 times 12 is 24.
Then 35 take away 24 is 11. So the round bracket is worth 11.
Now we see 6 of 11. What does the little word of mean in maths?

ask.ifNot: In maths, of means lots of. So 6 of 11 is 6 times 11.

beats.say: Of means times. 6 times 11 is 66.
Now finish the square bracket. 15 plus 66 is 81.
Last job. 178 take away 81. Take away 80 first to get 98, then 1 more to get 97.
We went from the inside out: the round bracket, then the of, then the square bracket, then the take away.
Two sums with a gap between them. We work out each side, then choose the sign that fits.
Left side. Times first. 17 times 10 is 170, and 17 times 7 is 119. So 17 times 17 is 289.
Now add the 45. 289 plus 45 is 334. That is the left side.
Right side: 16 times 14 plus 89. Which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus. So 16 times 14 comes first, and the 89 is added after.

beats.say: 16 times 10 is 160, and 16 times 4 is 64. So 16 times 14 is 224.
Add the 89. 224 plus 89 is 313. That is the right side.
Now compare 334 with 313. Which is bigger?

ask.ifNot: Both have 3 hundreds, so look at the tens. 334 has 3 tens and 313 has only 1 ten. So 334 is bigger.

beats.say: 334 is more than 313. So the left side is greater, and the sign is the greater than sign.
So: work out each side fully, times before plus, and only then compare.
We are asked which bracket makes this sum equal 40. The only way to know is to test each bracket in turn.
First, a bracket round 16 plus 24. That bracket is worth 40. Then 40 divided by 4 is 10, and 6 times 2 is 12.
10 plus 12 is 22. That is not 40, so cross this bracket off.
Second, a bracket round 4 plus 6 times 2. Inside it, times goes first. 6 times 2 is 12, and 4 plus 12 is 16.
So we would need 24 divided by 16. That does not share out evenly, so it cannot give 40. Cross it off.
Third, a bracket round 16 plus 24 divided by 4. Inside the bracket, what goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, divide goes before plus. So 24 divided by 4 comes first.

beats.say: 24 divided by 4 is 6, and 16 plus 6 is 22. Then add the 12 from 6 times 2. 22 plus 12 is 34. Not 40.
We tested all three brackets. None of them makes 40. So the answer is none of these.
That is the trap here. Do not pick a bracket just because it looks neat. Test every choice, and be brave enough to say none of these.
This sum should come to 40, but it needs one bracket to make it true. Let us find where the bracket goes.
First, try it with no bracket at all. Times first: 3 times 25 is 75. Then 75 take away 13, plus 4, comes to 66. Too big.
We want 40, not 66. So the 3 must multiply something smaller than 25. Which bracket does that?

ask.ifNot: A bracket round 25 minus 13 is worth less than 25. Then the 3 multiplies a smaller number.

beats.say: Try it. Bracket first. 25 take away 13 is 12.
Then the times. 3 times 12 is 36.
Then the plus. 36 plus 4 is 40. That is our number!
So the bracket goes round 25 minus 13.
What about the other brackets? Round 13 plus 4, we get 75 take away 17, which is 58. Round all three numbers, we get 3 times 16, which is 48. Neither is 40.
The key idea: a bracket changes which job is done first. Try it, work it through, and see if it lands on the target.
We add 2012 and 689. Then we take away a mystery number, and 1789 is left. What is the mystery number?
First find the sum. 2012 is 2000 and 12. 2000 plus 689 is 2689. Then 12 more makes 2701.
We have 2701, and we want to be left with 1789. How do we find what to take away?

ask.ifNot: The number to take away is the gap between 2701 and 1789. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: Find the gap by counting up from 1789. Add 11 to reach 1800. Add 200 to reach 2000. Then add 701 to reach 2701.
Now add up the three hops. 11 and 200 and 701 make 912.
So we must subtract 912.
Check by adding back. 1789 plus 912 takes us to 2701 again. It fits.
So: do the sum first. Then the number to take away is the gap between what you have and what you want.
A long sum, with a bracket inside a bracket. No need to panic. We start at the innermost bracket.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: Brackets go first, and the innermost bracket goes first of all. That is the round one: 8 plus 5 minus 6.

beats.say: Inside the round bracket, go left to right. 8 plus 5 is 13, and 13 take away 6 is 7.
Now the curly bracket is 7 times 2, which is 14.
The brackets are gone. Next comes the times. 7 times 7 is 49.
Only plus and minus are left. How do we go now?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go left to right, like reading. Only the 36 is taken away. The 2 and the 14 are added.

beats.say: 49 take away 36 is 13. Then 13 plus 2 is 15.
And 15 plus 14 is 29.
So: innermost bracket, then the outer bracket, then times, then plus and minus from left to right.
A bracket inside a bracket. We start in the very middle and work our way out.
Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: The inner bracket goes first. And inside it, divide goes before minus. So we begin with 72 divided by 8.

beats.say: 72 divided by 8 is 9. Then 9 take away 5 is 4. So the inner bracket is worth 4.
Now the outer bracket: 12 plus 4 times 3. Careful, here is a trap. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times goes before plus. So 4 times 3 comes first.

beats.say: 4 times 3 is 12. Then 12 plus 12 is 24. So the whole bracket is worth 24.
Last job: 192 divided by 24. Think in times. 24 times what makes 192?
24 times 10 is 240, which is too big. Take away 2 lots of 24, which is 48, and we land on 192. So 24 times 8 is 192.
So 192 divided by 24 is 8.
The other trap is dividing 192 by the first 12 straight away. The whole bracket must be finished before we divide.
So: inner bracket, then outer bracket, then the divide.
This sum should come to 17, and one bracket will make it true. Let us find where it goes.
With no bracket: 80 divided by 10 is 8, and 2 times 3 is 6. Then 8 plus 6 plus 12 is 26. Too big.
We need 17. The 12 at the end is added on, so the rest must make just 5. How can 80 be divided to give something as small as 5?

ask.ifNot: The bigger the number we divide by, the smaller the answer. So the bracket should make the number after the divide sign bigger than 10.

beats.say: So put the bracket straight after the divide sign, round 10 plus 2 times 3.
Inside the bracket, times goes first. 2 times 3 is 6, and 10 plus 6 is 16.
80 divided by 16 is 5, because 16 times 5 is 80.
And 5 plus 12 is 17. That is our number!
So the bracket goes round 10 plus 2 times 3.
The key idea: a bracket after a divide sign makes a bigger number to divide by, and that makes the answer smaller.
A long adding sum on the left, a times sum on the right, and a box between them. We work out each side, then pick the sign.
Left side. Adding is easier when we look for friendly pairs. 2 and 8 make 10. 4 and 6 make 10.
Then 12 and 16 make 28. So the left side is 10 plus 10 plus 28, which is 48.
Right side: 8 times 7. Do you remember it?

ask.ifNot: 8 times 7 is 56. Here is a way to remember it: 5, 6, 7, 8. 56 is 7 times 8.

beats.say: 8 times 7 is 56.
Now compare 48 with 56. Which is true?

ask.ifNot: 48 has 4 tens and 56 has 5 tens. So 48 is the smaller one, and the pointed end of the sign faces it.

beats.say: 48 is less than 56. So the sign in the box is the less than sign.
So: work out each side fully, and only then compare.
Lots of numbers in this story! We take it one step at a time. First, how many pencils does the school buy?

board.text: 15 boxes of 24.  12 teachers keep 8 each.  6 classes.

beats.say: 15 boxes with 24 in each is 15 times 24. 10 times 24 is 240, and 5 times 24 is 120. Together, 360 pencils.
Now the teachers. 12 teachers keep 8 pencils each. How many pencils is that?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 12 teachers keeps 8. So that is 12 lots of 8, not just 12 pencils.

beats.say: 12 times 8 is 96. So the teachers keep 96 pencils.
Take those away. 360 take away 96. Take away 100 to get 260, then give 4 back. 264 pencils are left.
These 264 pencils are shared equally among 6 classes. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: The classes share only what is left after the teachers take theirs. That is 264, so we need 264 divided by 6.

beats.say: Split 264 into 240 and 24. 240 divided by 6 is 40, and 24 divided by 6 is 4.
40 and 4 make 44. So each class gets 44 pencils.
The plan was: find the total, take away what the teachers keep, then share the rest. One step at a time.
Two brackets in this one. Brackets go first, so we deal with them one at a time.
Look inside the first bracket: 10 minus 2 times 3. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times goes before minus. So 2 times 3 comes first.

beats.say: 2 times 3 is 6, and 10 take away 6 is 4. The first bracket is worth 4.
The second bracket is quick. 7 take away 4 is 3.
Write the sum again, with 4 and 3 in place of the brackets.
Now there is a divide, a plus and a times. Which one waits until the end?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times go before plus. So the plus waits until the end.

beats.say: 48 divided by 4 is 12. And 5 times 3 is 15.
Now the plus. 12 plus 15 is 27.
So: brackets first, with times before minus inside them. Then divide and times. Then plus.
Four sums, and we want the one with the smallest value. We cannot tell just by looking, so we work out all four.
First one. Bracket first: 30 take away 6 is 24. Then 24 divided by 3 is 8, and 8 plus 2 is 10.
Second one: 6 plus 18 divided by a bracket. The bracket, 3 times 2, is 6. Then which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide goes before plus. So 18 divided by 6 comes first.

beats.say: 18 divided by 6 is 3, and 6 plus 3 is 9.
Third one. Bracket first: 3 plus 5 is 8. Then times before minus: 4 times 8 is 32. And 40 take away 32 is 8.
Fourth one. Bracket first: 2 plus 3 is 5. Then 50 divided by 5 is 10, and 10 plus 1 is 11.
Our four values are 10, then 9, then 8, then 11. Which is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: Put them in order from small to big: 8, then 9, then 10, then 11. The smallest is 8.

beats.say: 8 is the smallest, and it came from the third sum.
The trap is the second sum. It comes to 9, which is close, but the third one is smaller still. Always work out every choice.
A train story with lots of numbers. We need two things: how many seats there are, and how many people are on the train now.

board.text: 12 coaches of 72 seats.  598 on, 135 off, 210 on.

beats.say: Seats first. 12 coaches with 72 seats each. 10 times 72 is 720, and 2 times 72 is 144. Together, 864 seats.
Now the passengers. The train starts with 598. Then 135 get off and 210 get on. Which sum shows that?

ask.ifNot: Getting off means fewer people, so take away 135. Getting on means more people, so add 210.

beats.say: People who get off are taken away. People who get on are added.
598 take away 135 is 463. Then 463 plus 210 is 673. So 673 passengers are on the train now.
864 seats and 673 passengers, each in one seat. How do we find the empty seats?

ask.ifNot: Every passenger fills one seat. So take the 673 passengers who are on the train now away from the 864 seats.

beats.say: 864 take away 673. Take away 600 to get 264. Then take away 73 more to get 191.
So 191 seats are empty.
The trap is using the 598 from the first station. People got off and on after that, so we must use the new number, 673.
A shopkeeper story. We need the money he paid, the money he got, and then the gap between the two.

board.text: Buys 9 dozen at 4 rupees each. 12 go bad. Sells at 6 rupees.

beats.say: How many bananas did he buy? 9 dozen is 9 times 12, which is 108.
He paid 4 rupees for each one. 100 times 4 is 400, and 8 times 4 is 32. So he paid 432 rupees.
Then 12 bananas go bad. How many can he sell?

ask.ifNot: The 12 bad bananas are thrown away. So take 12 from 108, which leaves 96 to sell.

beats.say: 108 take away 12 is 96. He sells 96 bananas.
Each one sells for 6 rupees. 90 times 6 is 540, and 6 times 6 is 36. So he gets 576 rupees.
He paid 432 and he got 576. How do we find how much more he got?

ask.ifNot: How much more means the gap. Take what he paid, 432, away from what he got, 576.

beats.say: 576 take away 432 is 144. So he gets 144 rupees more than he paid.
Watch the trap. He paid for all 108 bananas, even the bad ones. But he only sold 96. Keep those two numbers apart.
This looks like a lot of hard multiplying. But there is a clever shortcut hiding in it. Let us hunt for it.
Look at the first part: 25 times 37 times 4. Two of those numbers make a lovely round number. Which two?

ask.ifNot: Try 25 and 4. Four 25s make exactly one hundred, and multiplying by a hundred is the easiest job of all.

beats.say: 25 times 4 is 100. We may multiply in any order, so the first part is 100 times 37.
Now read it in words. It says: 100 lots of 37, take away 99 lots of 37.
If you have 100 lots of something and you take away 99 lots, how many lots are left?

ask.ifNot: 100 take away 99 is 1. So just 1 lot of 37 is left.

beats.say: 100 take away 99 is 1. So just one lot of 37 is left.
And one lot of 37 is 37. No long multiplying needed!
Careful with the trap. It is 99 lots that are taken away, not 100. So the answer is not 0. One 37 is left over.
The key idea: before you multiply big numbers, look for a friendly pair, and look for the same number on both sides of the minus.
500 laddoos go into boxes of 12. Some will be left over, and those are shared among 4 children.

board.text: 500 laddoos in boxes of 12. Left-overs to 4 children.

beats.say: How many full boxes? Let us build up in twelves. 12 times 40 is 480.
One more box makes 492. Another box would make 504, which is more than 500. So there are 41 full boxes.
41 boxes use up 492 laddoos. How many are left over?

ask.ifNot: Take the 492 that are packed away from the 500. That leaves 8.

beats.say: 500 take away 492 is 8. So 8 laddoos are left over.
8 shared equally among 4 children is 8 divided by 4, which is 2. Each child gets 2 laddoos.
Careful with the trap. The children do not share all 500 laddoos. And 8 is not the final answer either. Only the left-overs are shared.
So: find the full boxes, find what is left over, then share that.
Three kinds of bracket, one inside the other, like boxes inside boxes. We open the smallest box first.
Start in the round bracket: 18 plus 12 divided by 3. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, divide goes before plus. So 12 divided by 3 comes first.

beats.say: 12 divided by 3 is 4, and 18 plus 4 is 22. The round bracket is worth 22.
Next, the square bracket. 60 take away 22 is 38.
Careful here. We take the whole 38 away from 100. We do not take away 60 and then 22, one after the other.
Now the curly bracket. 100 take away 38 is 62.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: Look at the end of the sum. There is still a divide by 2 waiting outside the brackets.

beats.say: Half of 62 is 31.
So: round bracket, square bracket, curly bracket, and then whatever is waiting outside.
Asha earns money, spends some, and saves the rest. We want to know how many weeks it takes her to save 18,000 rupees.

board.text: Earns 500 a day, 6 days a week. Spends 1,800 a week.

beats.say: First, how much does she earn in a week? 6 days at 500 rupees a day. 6 times 5 is 30, so 6 times 500 is 3,000.
She spends 1,800 of that each week. How much does she save in a week?

ask.ifNot: Saving is what is left after spending. Take 1,800 away from 3,000, and 1,200 is left.

beats.say: 3,000 take away 1,800 is 1,200. So she saves 1,200 rupees every week.
Now, how many weeks to reach 18,000? Which number do we divide 18,000 by?

ask.ifNot: Only the money she saves builds up. So we count how many lots of 1,200 make 18,000.

beats.say: Count up in lots of 1,200. 10 weeks give 12,000. That leaves 6,000 still to save.
5 more weeks give that 6,000, because 5 times 1,200 is 6,000.
10 weeks and 5 weeks make 15 weeks. She needs 15 weeks.
The trap is choosing which number to divide by. It is the saving each week that counts, not the spending, and not the pay for one day.
A long sum with a bracket, some times, a divide, a minus and a plus. We take it in the proper order.
Bracket first. 9 take away 4 is 5.
Now look at the minus and the plus. They cut the sum into three chunks. We work out each chunk on its own.
First chunk: 7 times 8 is 56. Second chunk: 6 times 5 is 30.
Third chunk: 20 divided by 5 times 2. Careful, this is the trap. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times are equal partners, so we go left to right. The divide comes first here: 20 divided by 5.

beats.say: Left to right. 20 divided by 5 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8.
Now put the three chunks back with their signs. 56 minus 30 plus 8.
Left to right again. 56 take away 30 is 26, and 26 plus 8 is 34.
So: brackets, then times and divide from left to right, then plus and minus from left to right.
A hall full of chairs, and then two things change: the number of rows, and the number of chairs in each row.

board.text: 28 rows of 35 chairs. 15 rows go. 6 more chairs a row.

beats.say: First the rows. 15 rows are taken away from 28. 28 take away 15 is 13 rows.
Now 6 more chairs are added to each row that is left. How many chairs are in one row now?

ask.ifNot: Each row had 35 chairs and gets 6 more. 35 plus 6 is 41.

beats.say: 35 plus 6 is 41. So each row now has 41 chairs.
13 rows with 41 chairs in each. Which sum gives all the chairs?

ask.ifNot: There are 13 rows left, and every one of them has 41 chairs. So we need 13 times 41.

beats.say: 13 times 41. 10 times 41 is 410, and 3 times 41 is 123.
410 plus 123 is 533. So there are 533 chairs in the hall now.
Careful with the trap. The 6 extra chairs go into every one of the 13 rows. It is not just 6 chairs for the whole hall.
So: find the new number of rows, find the new chairs in a row, then multiply.
A farmer packs 1,000 mangoes, first into crates and then into baskets. We need the number of baskets.

board.text: 1,000 mangoes. 25 crates of 2 dozen. Baskets of 50.

beats.say: Each crate holds 2 dozen mangoes. How many is that?

ask.ifNot: A dozen is 12. So 2 dozen is 2 times 12, which is 24.

beats.say: 2 dozen is 2 times 12, which is 24 mangoes in each crate.
Now 25 crates of 24. 20 times 24 is 480, and 5 times 24 is 120. Together, 600 mangoes go into crates.
Take those from the 1,000. 1,000 take away 600 leaves 400 mangoes.
These 400 go into baskets of 50. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: Only the mangoes that are left go into baskets. That is 400, so we need 400 divided by 50.

beats.say: How many fifties are in 400? 2 fifties make 100. So 400 needs 4 times as many, which is 8 fifties.
So he needs 8 baskets.
The plan: mangoes in one crate, mangoes in all the crates, mangoes left, and then the baskets.
We must put one pair of brackets into this sum so that it comes to 14.
First, what is it worth with no brackets? Times first: 4 times 5 is 20. Then 6 plus 20, take away 3, comes to 23.
23 is too big. We want 14. So the brackets must make something smaller. Which part can we make smaller?

ask.ifNot: A bracket round 4 times 5 changes nothing, because times goes first anyway. But a bracket round 5 minus 3 makes the 4 multiply a smaller number.

beats.say: Try it. Bracket first: 5 take away 3 is 2.
Then the times. 4 times 2 is 8.
Then the plus. 6 plus 8 is 14. That is our target!
So the brackets go round 5 minus 3.
A bracket round 6 plus 4 would give 10 times 5, take away 3, which is 47. Far too big.
The key idea: brackets only matter when they change which job goes first.
Riya may put in one pair of brackets, and she wants the smallest value she can get. Let us think like detectives.
With no brackets: 36 divided by 6 is 6, and 3 times 2 is 6. Then 6 plus 6 is 12.
To get less than 12, here is the big idea. What happens when you divide 36 by a bigger number?

ask.ifNot: Share 36 sweets among more children and each child gets fewer. Dividing by a bigger number gives a smaller answer.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number we can make straight after the divide sign. Try a bracket round 6 plus 3. That makes 9.
36 divided by 9 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8. That is smaller than 12. But can we do better?
Make the bracket longer: 6 plus 3 times 2. Inside it, times goes first. 3 times 2 is 6, and 6 plus 6 is 12.
Now we are dividing by 12. And 36 divided by 12 is 3.
What about a bracket at the front, round 36 divided by 6 plus 3? That gives 9 times 2, which is 18. Bigger, not smaller.
So the smallest value is 3. The key idea: to make a division small, make the number you divide by as big as you can.
Two empty boxes, and each needs a sign. The finished sum must come to 9. We test the choices, and we always follow the order rules.
Try plus then divide first: 12 plus 6 divided by 2. Which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide goes before plus. So 6 divided by 2 comes first.

beats.say: 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 12 plus 3 is 15. Not 9. This is the trap: adding first, from the left, seems to give 9, but that breaks the rule.
Now try minus then divide: 12 minus 6 divided by 2. Again the divide goes first. 6 divided by 2 is 3.
12 take away 3 is 9. That is our number!
A quick check on the other two. 12 divided by 6, plus 2, is 4. And 12 minus 6, plus 2, is 8. Neither is 9.
So the signs are minus, then divide.
When you test signs, work the sum out by the rules, not just from left to right.
We have three signs, plus, minus and times, to use once each. We want the biggest answer we can make.
Times makes numbers grow the most. So where should the times go?

ask.ifNot: 8 and 2 are the biggest pair of neighbours, so multiplying them gives the biggest product. 2 times 3 is only 6, and 3 times 1 is only 3.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16. That is far more than 2 times 3, or 3 times 1.
Now the plus and the minus go in front of the 3 and the 1. Which way round is better?

ask.ifNot: Add the bigger number and take away the smaller one. So plus 3, minus 1.

beats.say: Add the bigger one, take away the smaller one. So the sum is 8 times 2, plus 3, minus 1.
Times first gives 16. Then 16 plus 3 is 19, and 19 take away 1 is 18.
Check a rival, with the times in the middle: 8 plus 2 times 3, minus 1. That is 8 plus 6, minus 1, which is only 13.
Careful with a trap. Reading that rival from left to right, as 10 times 3, gives a number that is too big. Times must go first.
So the greatest result is 18. Put the times where the numbers are biggest, add the bigger number, and take away the smaller.
The seller sells half of his mangoes and 2 more. Then he does the same again. In the end 8 are left. How many did he start with?

board.text: Sells half and 2 more, twice. 8 left. Start = ?

beats.say: We know the end of the story, not the beginning. So we work backwards, undoing one sale at a time.
Undo the afternoon. He sold half, and then 2 more, and 8 were left. Which do we undo first?

ask.ifNot: The 2 extra mangoes were sold last, so they go back first. After that we double.

beats.say: Put the 2 back: 8 plus 2 is 10. That 10 is the half he kept, so double it. 10 times 2 is 20.
So there were 20 mangoes after the morning. Now undo the morning in exactly the same way.
Put the 2 back: 20 plus 2 is 22. Then double: 22 times 2 is 44.
Let us check by going forwards. Half of 44 is 22. Selling 22 and 2 more leaves 20.
Half of 20 is 10. Selling 10 and 2 more leaves 8. It matches the story!
The trap is doubling before adding the 2 back. Undo things in the opposite order: the last thing done is the first thing undone. So the start was 44.
Asha and Bela have 60 stickers together. Asha gives Bela 8, and then they have the same number. How many did Asha start with?

board.text: Asha + Bela = 60.  Asha gives 8.  Then equal.

beats.say: Here is something useful. When Asha gives stickers to Bela, no sticker is lost. So the total is still 60.
At the end the two girls have the same number, and 60 altogether. How many does each have?

ask.ifNot: Two equal shares that make 60. Half of 60 is 30, so each girl has 30.

beats.say: 60 shared equally between 2 is 30. So at the end, each girl has 30.
Asha has 30 after giving 8 away. So before she gave them, did she have more than 30, or fewer?

ask.ifNot: She gave 8 away to get down to 30. So before that she had 8 more than 30.

beats.say: Put the 8 back. 30 plus 8 is 38. Asha had 38 stickers at first.
Check. Bela had 60 take away 38, which is 22. After getting 8, she has 30. And Asha, after giving 8, has 30 too. Equal!
So: find what each girl has at the end, then undo the giving. Asha started with 38.
500 oranges go into boxes of 24. The last box will not be full. How many more oranges would fill it?

board.text: 500 oranges, boxes of 24. Last box needs ? more

beats.say: First, the full boxes. 24 times 10 is 240. So 24 times 20 is 480.
One more box would need 504 oranges, and that is more than 500. So 20 boxes are full.
20 full boxes use 480 oranges. How many oranges are left over for the last box?

ask.ifNot: Take the 480 that are packed away from 500. That leaves 20 oranges.

beats.say: 500 take away 480 is 20. So the last box holds 20 oranges.
Is 20 our answer?

choices: No: find how many more make 24
ask.ifNot: Read the question again. It asks how many more oranges are needed to fill the box, and a full box holds 24.

beats.say: A full box holds 24, and this one has 20. 24 take away 20 is 4. He needs 4 more oranges.
Funny thing: there are 20 full boxes, and also 20 oranges left over. Do not mix them up. The question wants the gap up to 24.
So: find the left-overs, then find how many more make a full box.
Four times sums, and we want the greatest. Multiplying all four out would take ages. Let us look for a pattern instead.
Add the two numbers in each pair. 47 and 53. 49 and 51. 48 and 52. 50 and 50. What do you notice?

ask.ifNot: 47 and 53 make 100. 49 and 51 make 100. 48 and 52 make 100. And 50 and 50 make 100 too.

beats.say: Every pair adds up to 100. So the real question is: with the same total, which pair gives the biggest product?
Try it with small numbers that add up to 10. 5 times 5 is 25. 4 times 6 is 24. 3 times 7 is 21.
Which small pair gave the biggest product?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 5 gave 25, the biggest. The closer together the two numbers are, the bigger the product.

beats.say: The closer the two numbers, the bigger the product. And 50 and 50 are as close as can be.
So 50 times 50 is the greatest. 5 times 5 is 25, so 50 times 50 is 2500.
Check the nearest rival. 49 times 50 is 2450, and one more 49 makes 2499. That is just 1 less than 2500.
The trap is picking the pair with the biggest single number, 53. Its partner is small, so that product is the smallest. The winner is 50 times 50.
One empty box. Which sign makes the sum come to 12? We test, and we follow the order rules every time.
Try divide: 6 plus 12 divided by 3 times 2. Which part waits until the end?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times go before plus. So the 6 plus at the front waits until the end.

beats.say: 12 divided by 3 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8. Then 6 plus 8 is 14. Not 12.
That was the trap. Going left to right from the very start seems to give 12, but the plus must wait its turn.
Now try minus: 6 plus 12 minus 3 times 2. Times goes first. 3 times 2 is 6.
Left to right now. 6 plus 12 is 18, and 18 take away 6 is 12. That is our number!
The other two signs make it far too big. Plus gives 24, and times gives 78.
So the sign in the box is minus.
When you test a sign, work the whole sum out by the rules: times and divide before plus and minus.
Four sums, each with brackets. In one of them the brackets are not really needed. Which one?

board.text: Where can the brackets go without changing the value?

beats.say: Remember what brackets do. They say: do me first. So brackets are not needed when that part would go first anyway.
Look at 12 minus, bracket, 4 times 2. If the brackets were not there, what would go first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before minus. So 4 times 2 goes first, even with no brackets.

beats.say: Times goes first anyway. With brackets or without, it is 12 take away 8, which is 4. The value does not change.
Test another. 12 minus, bracket, 4 plus 2, is 12 take away 6, which is 6. Without brackets we go left to right and get 10. It changed.
Next: bracket 12 minus 4, times 2. That is 8 times 2, which is 16. Without the brackets, times goes first and we get 4. It changed.
Last one. 12 divided by, bracket, 4 plus 2, is 2. Without the brackets, divide goes first and we get 5. It changed too.
So only the first one stays the same.
The key idea: brackets can go when they only wrap a times or a divide that would have gone first anyway.
Rohit buys 10 things, some pencils and some pens, and pays exactly 60 rupees. How many are pens?

board.text: Pencil 4 rupees, pen 9 rupees. 10 things cost 60.

beats.say: Here is a clever way in. Pretend all 10 are pencils, the cheaper ones. 10 times 4 is 40 rupees.
But he paid 60, not 40. That is 20 rupees more.
Where does the extra 20 come from? Each time we swap a pencil for a pen, how much does the bill go up?

ask.ifNot: A pen costs 9 and a pencil costs 4. Swapping one for the other adds the gap, 9 take away 4, which is 5 rupees.

beats.say: A pen costs 5 rupees more than a pencil. So every swap adds 5 rupees.
How many swaps make 20 rupees? 20 divided by 5 is 4. So 4 of the things are pens.
Check. 4 pens cost 36 rupees. The other 6 things are pencils, and they cost 24 rupees.
36 plus 24 is 60. Exactly what he paid.
Careful at the end: 6 is the number of pencils. The question asks for pens, and that is 4.
Kiran should have divided her number by 6. But she multiplied it by 6 instead, and got 432. What should her answer have been?
First we need Kiran's number. She multiplied it by 6 to get 432. How do we go back?

ask.ifNot: Divide undoes times. So to undo multiplying by 6, we divide 432 by 6.

beats.say: Divide undoes times. So we need 432 divided by 6. Split 432 into 420 and 12.
420 divided by 6 is 70, and 12 divided by 6 is 2. So her number was 72.
Is 72 the answer?

ask.ifNot: 72 is only the number she started with. She was supposed to divide it by 6, and that is still to do.

beats.say: Now do what she was meant to do: 72 divided by 6. 60 is 10 sixes, and the other 12 is 2 more sixes.
10 and 2 make 12. Kiran should have got 12.
So we divided by 6 twice: once to undo her slip, and once to do the real job.
Nine numbers to add on the left, a times sum on the right, and a box between them. We find each side, then pick the sign.
Adding nine numbers one by one is slow. Here is a trick: make pairs. What do 1 and 9 make?

ask.ifNot: 1 plus 9 is 10. And tens are lovely to add.

beats.say: 1 and 9 make 10. So do 2 and 8, 3 and 7, and 4 and 6. That is four tens, which is 40.
The 5 in the middle has no partner. Add it on: 40 plus 5 is 45. The left side is 45.
Right side. 5 times 7 is 35.
Compare 45 with 35. Which is true?

ask.ifNot: 45 has 4 tens and 35 has only 3 tens. So 45 is bigger, and the open mouth of the sign faces the 45.

beats.say: 45 is greater than 35. So the sign in the box is the greater than sign.
So: work out both sides first, then compare. And when you add a long list, hunt for pairs that make 10.
The bottle holds 150 millilitres of syrup, and 25 millilitres are taken each day. How many days will it last?
Each day uses up one lot of 25. So what do we need to find?

ask.ifNot: Every day takes one lot of 25 out of the bottle. So we count how many lots of 25 fit into 150.

beats.say: That is a division. 150 divided by 25.
Let us count up in 25s, one for each day. 25, 50, 75, 100.
Keep going. 125, 150. We have reached the full bottle. That was 6 lots of 25.
So 150 divided by 25 is 6. The syrup lasts for 6 days.
Check by multiplying. 6 times 25 is 150. It fits.
So when something is used up in equal amounts, divide the total by the amount used each time.
Three baskets, A, B and C. We only know C for sure: it has 22 oranges. So we start there and build up.
Basket A has 16 more than C. 22 plus 16 is 38. So A has 38 oranges.
Now basket B. Read carefully: B has 12 more than the sum of A and C. So what must we find first?

ask.ifNot: The sum of A and C means A and C added together. B is compared with both baskets together, not with one of them.

beats.say: This is the trap in the question. B is compared with A and C together. 38 plus 22 is 60.
B has 12 more than that. 60 plus 12 is 72. So B has 72 oranges.
Now add all three baskets. We already know that A and C make 60. So we need 60 plus 72.
60 plus 72 is 132. The fruit seller bought 132 oranges.
So: start from the basket you know, build the others one at a time, and read each clue slowly.
The shopkeeper has 6 gross of pencils, and each box holds one dozen. How many boxes does he fill?

board.text: 6 gross of pencils.   Each box holds 1 dozen.

beats.say: First, what is a gross?

ask.ifNot: A gross is 12 dozen. That is 12 lots of 12.

beats.say: A gross is 12 dozen. Let us write that down.
Now look. Each box holds exactly one dozen. So one gross fills 12 boxes.
He has 6 gross. Which sum gives the number of boxes?

ask.ifNot: Each gross fills 12 boxes, and there are 6 gross. So we need 6 lots of 12.

beats.say: 6 times 12. 6 times 10 is 60, and 6 times 2 is 12. Together, 72.
So 72 boxes will be packed.
We could have counted every pencil. 6 gross is 864 pencils, and 864 divided by 12 is 72 as well. But thinking in dozens was much quicker.
So when the units match, like dozens and boxes of a dozen, work in those units. 72 boxes it is.
Two mystery numbers. Each has three digits. One ends in 7 and the other ends in 8. Which choice could be their product?
We cannot multiply, because we do not know the numbers. But we can be detectives. Here are the four choices.
Clue one. The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. So what must this product end in?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 8 is 56, and 56 ends in 6. So the product must end in 6.

beats.say: It must end in 6. So 10552 is out, because it ends in 2.
Clue two: the size. Each number has three digits, so each is at least 100. And 100 times 100 is 10000, which has five digits.
So the product has at least five digits. 9786 has only four, so it is too small. Cross it off.
Each number is also less than 1000. And 1000 times 1000 is 1000000, which has seven digits. So our product has fewer than seven digits.
9950006 has seven digits, so it is too big. Cross it off.
Only one choice is left. It ends in 6 and it is the right size. So the product can be 308256.
The key idea: you can rule answers out without multiplying. Check the last digit, and check how many digits there should be.
Here is our sum. Plus, times, minus and divide, all in one line. The BODMAS rule tells us the order.
Which two jobs go first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide go before plus and minus. So 5 times 4, and 6 divided by 2, go first.

beats.say: Box them both. Notice that the divide only touches the 6 just in front of it, not the whole sum.
5 times 4 is 20. And 6 divided by 2 is 3.
Write the sum again, with 20 and 3 where the boxes were.
Left to right now. 6 plus 20 is 26.
And 26 take away 3 is 23.
The trap is going straight along from the left, with 6 plus 5 first. That gives a different answer. Times and divide must jump the queue.
So: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right.
This sum should come to 40. As it stands, it does not. One bracket will fix it, and we must find where it goes.
First, with no bracket. Times first: 5 times 7 is 35. Then 35 plus 3, take away 10, is 28. Too small.
We need a bigger answer, 40. So the 5 should multiply something bigger than 7. Which bracket makes that happen?

ask.ifNot: A bracket round 5 times 7 changes nothing, because times goes first anyway. A bracket round 7 plus 3 makes the 5 multiply 10 instead of 7.

beats.say: Try it. Bracket first: 7 plus 3 is 10.
Then the times. 5 times 10 is 50.
Then the minus. 50 take away 10 is 40. That is our number!
So the bracket goes round 7 plus 3.
One more choice to check. A bracket round 7 plus 3 minus 10 is worth 0, and 5 times 0 is 0. No good.
The key idea: the bracket has to make the adding happen before the multiplying. So it goes round 7 plus 3.
A sum with a bracket at the end. Brackets go first, so we begin inside it.
Inside the bracket: 2 times 4 minus 15 divided by 3. Which jobs go first in there?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times and divide go before minus. So 2 times 4, and 15 divided by 3, go first.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. And 15 divided by 3 is 5.
Finish the bracket. 8 take away 5 is 3. So the bracket is worth 3.
Now outside the bracket: 9 minus 3 times 2 plus 3. Careful, this is the trap. What goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before minus, even though the minus is written first. So 3 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6. Now the sum is 9 minus 6 plus 3.
Left to right. 9 take away 6 is 3. Then 3 plus 3 is 6.
One more trap. The sign in front of the bracket is a plus. So the bracket's 3 is added at the end, not taken away.
So: bracket first, then times and divide, then plus and minus from left to right.
Four times sums joined by plus and minus. We could work out each one. But first, look closely. Which number keeps coming back?

ask.ifNot: Every part has a 7 in it: 11 times 7, 13 times 7, 7 times 6 and 2 times 7.

beats.say: Every part has a 7. So each part is just a number of sevens: 11 sevens, 13 sevens, 6 sevens and 2 sevens.
So we can simply count sevens. But careful: one lot is taken away. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Look at the sign in front of 7 times 6. It is a minus. So those 6 sevens are taken away.

beats.say: 11 plus 13 is 24. Take away 6 to get 18. Add 2 to get 20. So there are 20 sevens altogether.
20 sevens. 2 times 7 is 14, so 20 times 7 is 140.
Let us check the long way. The four products are 77, 91, 42 and 14. The 42 is the one that is taken away.
77 plus 91 is 168. Take away 42 to get 126. Add 14 to get 140. The same answer.
So when the same number sits in every part, count how many of it you have. And watch for the minus: that part is taken away.
Three statements, and we check each one by the rules. Maybe one is true. Maybe none is. Let us find out.

board.text: Which one is correct by the BODMAS rule?

beats.say: First: 2 times 7 minus 5 equals 4. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before minus. So 2 times 7 comes first.

beats.say: 2 times 7 is 14, and 14 take away 5 is 9, not 4. So the first one is not true.
Second: 5 plus 5 times 25 equals 250. Times first again. 5 times 25 is 125.
Then 5 plus 125 is 130, not 250. Not true. The 250 comes from adding 5 and 5 first, and that breaks the rule.
Third: bracket 18 plus 7, divided by 7, equals 19. Bracket first: 18 plus 7 is 25.
25 divided by 7 is 3, with 4 left over. That is nowhere near 19. Not true.
All three are crossed off. So the answer is none of these.
Each statement hid a trap: it did the jobs in a different order from the rule. Brackets first, then times and divide, then plus and minus.
Two mystery numbers with three digits each. One ends in 8, the other ends in 7. Which choice could be their product?
We cannot multiply mystery numbers. But we can be detectives and rule choices out. Here they are.
Clue one: the last digit. The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. What is 8 times 7?

ask.ifNot: 8 times 7 is 56. So the product must end in 6.

beats.say: 8 times 7 is 56, so the product must end in 6. But 11558 ends in 8. Cross it off.
The other three all end in 6. So now we need clue two: the size.
The smallest the two numbers can be is 108 and 107. 108 times 100 is 10800, and 108 times 7 is 756.
Together that is 11556. So the product is at least 11556. But 10556 is smaller than that. Cross it off.
Both numbers are less than 1000, and 1000 times 1000 is 1000000. So the product is less than that. 9995006 is far bigger. Cross it off.
Only 36846 is left. It ends in 6 and it is the right size.
The sneaky one was 10556. It ends in 6, but it is just too small. So check the last digit and the size, both.
A bracket, a divide, a plus and a times. Brackets go first, so we begin inside.
Inside the bracket: 19 plus 3 times 2. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times goes before plus. So 3 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6, and 19 plus 6 is 25. The bracket is worth 25.
Now we have 25 divided by 5, plus 4 times 3. Here is the trap. What happens to the plus?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times go before plus. So the plus waits until both of them are done.

beats.say: The plus waits. 25 divided by 5 is 5. And 4 times 3 is 12.
Now the plus gets its turn. 5 plus 12 is 17.
If we had added the 5 and the 4 first, and then multiplied by 3, we would have got a different number. The 4 belongs to the times.
So: bracket first, with times before plus inside it. Then divide and times. The plus comes last.
A cinema hall with rows named by letters. To count the people, we first need to know how many rows there are.

board.text: Rows A to Q, 17 seats each. Rows A to H: 3 empty each.

beats.say: The rows go from A to Q. Count along the alphabet on your fingers. How many letters is that?

ask.ifNot: Q is the 17th letter of the alphabet. So rows A to Q make 17 rows.

beats.say: Q is the 17th letter, so there are 17 rows. And each row has 17 seats.
17 rows of 17 seats. 17 times 10 is 170, and 17 times 7 is 119. Together, 289 seats.
Now the empty seats. Rows A to H each have 3 empty, and H is the 8th letter. How many seats are empty?

ask.ifNot: Only rows A to H have empty seats. That is 8 rows, with 3 empty seats in each. So 8 times 3.

beats.say: 8 times 3 is 24. So 24 seats are empty.
Take the empty seats away from all the seats. 289 take away 24 is 265.
So 265 people are seated. The trap was in the letters: A to Q is 17 rows, and A to H is 8 rows. Count them carefully.
This sum should come to 13. One bracket will make it true. Where does it go?
First, with no bracket. 48 divided by 8 is 6. Then 6 take away 2 is 4, and 4 plus 5 is 9. Too small.
We need a bigger answer. Here is an idea. If we divide 48 by a smaller number, what happens to the answer?

ask.ifNot: Share 48 among fewer people and each one gets more. Dividing by a smaller number gives a bigger answer.

beats.say: So let us make the number after the divide sign smaller. Put the bracket round 8 minus 2.
Bracket first. 8 take away 2 is 6.
Then the divide. 48 divided by 6 is 8.
Then the plus. 8 plus 5 is 13. That is our number!
So the bracket goes round 8 minus 2.
A bracket round 48 divided by 8 changes nothing, because the divide goes first anyway. A bracket is only useful when it changes the order.
Five eights and four different signs! It looks like a riddle, but the BODMAS rule sorts it out.
Which two jobs go first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide go before plus and minus. So 8 times 8, and 8 divided by 8, go first.

beats.say: Box the times and the divide.
8 times 8 is 64. And 8 divided by 8 is 1.
Write the sum again, with 64 and 1 where the boxes were. The 8 at the front is still there.
Left to right now. 8 plus 64 is 72.
And 72 take away 1 is 71.
Two traps here. Going straight along from the left gives a different answer. And do not forget that first 8: it still has to be added.
So: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Two mystery numbers with three digits each. One ends in 7, the other ends in 6. Which choice could be their product?
We cannot multiply them, but we can rule choices out, like detectives. Here are the four.
Clue one: the last digit. 7 times 6 is 42. So what must the product end in?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 6 is 42, and 42 ends in 2. So the product must end in 2.

beats.say: It must end in 2. But 51276 ends in 6, so cross it off.
Clue two: the size. Each number has three digits, so each is at least 100. And 100 times 100 is 10000, which has five digits.
So the product has at least five digits. 1342 has only four. Too small, so cross it off.
Each number is also less than 1000. And 1000 times 1000 is 1000000, which has seven digits. So the product has fewer than seven digits.
9933012 has seven digits. Too big, so cross it off.
Only 312312 is left. It ends in 2, and it has six digits, which is just right.
The key idea: check the last digit, then count the digits. No long multiplying needed.
Three and a quarter dozen. That means 3 whole dozens, and then a quarter of a dozen more. We do each part.
One dozen is 12. So 3 dozen is 3 times 12, which is 36.
Now a quarter of a dozen. A quarter means one of 4 equal parts. So what is a quarter of 12?

ask.ifNot: Split 12 into 4 equal parts. 12 divided by 4 is 3. So a quarter of a dozen is 3.

beats.say: 12 divided by 4 is 3. So a quarter of a dozen is 3 articles.
Now put the two parts together. 36 plus 3 is 39.
Careful with the trap. A quarter does not mean add 4. It means divide by 4.
So: the whole dozens first, then the part of a dozen, then add them.
Three signs in one sum: a minus, a times and a plus. The trick is knowing where to start.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 3 times 7.

beats.say: Times is the boss here. It goes before plus and minus, so put a box round 3 times 7.
3 times 7 is 21. Write 21 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 48 take away 21.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 48 take away 21 is 27.
And now the plus. 27 plus 14 is 41.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a minus, a times and a plus.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes first, so 3 times 7 is our first job.

beats.say: Times is the boss here. It goes before plus and minus, so put a box round 3 times 7.
3 times 7 is 21. So 21 goes where the box was. The rest of the sum stays the same.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 25 take away 21.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 25 take away 21 is 4.
And now the plus. 4 plus 1 is 5.
The trap in this sum is the minus at the front. It looks like the place to start, but the times must go first.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is our sum. 62 take away 3. Look at the sign first. It is a minus, so we take away.
62 has only 2 ones, and we need to take away 3. So first take away 2, to land on the round number 60.
We have taken 2 so far, out of 3. How many more do we still have to take away?

ask.ifNot: 3 is 2 and 1. We have taken the 2, so 1 more is still to go.

beats.say: 3 is 2 and 1. The 2 is done, and the 1 is still waiting.
Now hop back 1 more from 60. That lands on 59.
So 62 take away 3 equals 59.
Check by adding back. 59 plus 3 makes 62, the number we started with.
So when there are not enough ones, hop back to the round number first, then take away what is left.
Here is our sum. 63 plus 43.
Big numbers are friendlier in pieces. So we split each one into its tens and its ones.
Start with the tens. What is 60 plus 40?

ask.ifNot: 6 tens and 4 tens make 10 tens. And 10 tens is 100.

beats.say: 6 tens and 4 tens make 10 tens. That is 100.
Now the ones. 3 plus 3 is 6.
Now put the two parts together. 100 and 6 make 106.
So 63 plus 43 equals 106.
A quick check. 106 take away 43 is 63, right where we started. It fits.
So the plan is: split into tens and ones, add the tens, add the ones, then join them.
Let us multiply 19 by 43.
19 is just 1 less than 20. And 20 is a much friendlier number to multiply by.
So start with 20 lots of 43. 2 times 43 is 86, so 20 times 43 is 860.
But we only want 19 lots, not 20. What do we do now?

ask.ifNot: 20 lots is one lot too many. One lot is 43, so we take away 43.

beats.say: Take away 43 in two hops. First 40, which leaves 820. Then 3 more, which leaves 817.
So 19 times 43 is 817.
A quick check on the last digit. 9 times 3 is 27, which ends in 7. Our answer ends in 7 too.
So when a number is 1 less than a round number, use the round number, then take one lot away.
Let us multiply 99 by 39. Look at the sign first. It is times, so we multiply.
99 is just 1 less than 100. And 100 is a much friendlier number to multiply by.
So start with 100 lots of 39. That is 3900.
But we only want 99 lots, not 100. What do we do now?

ask.ifNot: 100 lots is one lot too many. One lot is 39, so we take away 39.

beats.say: Take away 39 in two hops. First 30, which leaves 3870. Then 9 more, which leaves 3861.
There it is. 99 times 39 makes 3861.
A quick check on the last digit. 9 times 9 is 81, which ends in 1. Our answer ends in 1 too.
So when a number is 1 less than a round number, use the round number, then take one lot away.
Here is our sum. 97 take away 50. Look at the sign first. It is a minus, so we take away.
50 is a round number, full tens and no ones. So split the 97 into 90 and 7.
Take the tens away first. What is 90 take away 50?

ask.ifNot: 9 tens take away 5 tens leaves 4 tens. And 4 tens is 40.

beats.say: 9 tens take away 5 tens leaves 4 tens. That is 40.
The 7 ones were never touched, so put them back. 40 and 7 make 47.
There it is. 97 minus 50 leaves 47.
Let us check by going backwards. 47 plus 50 is 97. It fits.
So when you take away a round number, only the tens change. The ones stay as they are.
Let us multiply 3 by 3. Look at the sign first. It is times, so we multiply.
3 times 3 means 3 groups of 3. Picture 3 rows with 3 in each row.
Which adding sum shows 3 groups of 3?

ask.ifNot: 3 groups of 3 means the 3 is written 3 times, with plus signs in between.

beats.say: Add them up. 3 plus 3 plus 3 makes 9.
So 3 times 3 equals 9.
Count the squares in the picture if you like. 3 rows of 3, and there are 9 squares.
So times is a quick way of adding the same number again and again.
50 times 47. Let us work it out together. The sign is times, so we want 50 lots of 47, not 50 plus 47.
50 is half of 100. And multiplying by 100 is easy, so let us start there.
100 lots of 47 is 4700.
But we only want 50 lots, and 50 is half of 100. So what do we do with 4700?

ask.ifNot: 50 lots is half as many as 100 lots. So we need half of 4700.

beats.say: Halve it in two pieces. Half of 4000 is 2000, and half of 700 is 350.
Together, 2000 and 350 make 2350.
So 50 times 47 equals 2350.
Check by doubling. Two lots of 2350 make 4700 again. It fits.
So to multiply by 50, multiply by 100 and then halve.
15 plus 2. Let us work it out together.
15 is 10 and 5. Let us split it into its tens and its ones.
There is room in the ones place, so only the ones will change. What is 5 plus 2?

ask.ifNot: Start at 5 and count on 2 more. You land on 7.

beats.say: 5 ones and 2 ones make 7 ones.
The tens have not changed, so put them back. 10 and 7 make 17.
So 15 plus 2 equals 17.
A quick check. 17 take away 2 is 15, right where we started. It fits.
So when you add a small number and there is room in the ones, keep the tens and just add the ones.
Here is our sum. 98 plus 47.
Big numbers are friendlier in pieces. So we split each one into its tens and its ones.
Start with the tens. What is 90 plus 40?

ask.ifNot: 9 tens and 4 tens make 13 tens. And 13 tens is 130.

beats.say: 9 tens and 4 tens make 13 tens. That is 130.
Now the ones. 8 plus 7 is 15. That is more than 9, and that is fine. We just add it on.
Now put the two parts together. 130 and 15 make 145.
So 98 plus 47 equals 145.
Let us check by going backwards. 145 take away 47 brings us back to 98.
So the plan is: split into tens and ones, add the tens, add the ones, then join them.
Here is our sum. 63 plus 6. Look at the sign first. It is a plus, so we add.
63 is 60 and 3. Let us split it into its tens and its ones.
There is room in the ones place, so only the ones will change. What is 3 plus 6?

ask.ifNot: Start at 3 and count on 6 more. You land on 9.

beats.say: 3 ones and 6 ones make 9 ones.
The tens have not changed, so put them back. 60 and 9 make 69.
So 63 plus 6 equals 69.
A quick check. 69 take away 6 is 63, right where we started. It fits.
The plan: split off the ones, add the ones, then put the tens back.
7 minus 5. Let us work it out together. The sign is a minus, so we are taking away, not adding.
Picture a number line. We start at 7 and hop back 5 times, one hop for each one we take away.
Where do we land?

ask.ifNot: Start at 7 and hop back one at a time, 5 hops in all. You land on 2.

beats.say: So 7 take away 5 equals 2.
Check by adding back. 2 plus 5 makes 7, the number we started with.
So taking away means hopping back along the number line.
46 minus 41. Let us work it out together.
Look how close these two numbers are. So here is a neat way: ask how far it is from 41 up to 46.

spec.note: Count the hops from 41 up to 46

beats.say: Count the hops from 41 up to 46. How many are there?

ask.ifNot: Start at 41 and hop up one at a time until you reach 46. That takes 5 hops.

beats.say: 5 hops. So 41 and 5 more make 46.
So 46 minus 41 is 5.
The answer cannot be a big number here, because 46 and 41 are almost the same size.
So when two numbers are close together, count up from the smaller one to the bigger one.
75 times 45. Let us work it out together. Look at the sign first. It is times, so we multiply.
Too big to do in one go. So split 45 into 40 and 5, and do one piece at a time.
Start with the tens piece, 40. First, 75 times 4. 70 times 4 is 280, and 5 times 4 is 20. Together that makes 300.
40 is 4 tens. So what is 75 times 40?

ask.ifNot: 40 is ten times 4. So the answer is ten times 300, which is 300 with a 0 on the end.

beats.say: Ten times 300 is 3000. That is the first piece done.
Now the ones piece. 75 times 5. 70 times 5 is 350, and 5 times 5 is 25. Together that makes 375.
Add the two pieces. 3000 plus 375 is 3375.
There it is. 75 times 45 makes 3375.
A quick check on the last digit. 5 times 5 is 25, which ends in 5. Our answer ends in 5 too.
So the plan is: split one number into tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add.
Let us add 54 and 3.
54 is 50 and 4. Let us split it into its tens and its ones.
There is room in the ones place, so only the ones will change. What is 4 plus 3?

ask.ifNot: Start at 4 and count on 3 more. You land on 7.

beats.say: 4 ones and 3 ones make 7 ones.
The tens have not changed, so put them back. 50 and 7 make 57.
So 54 plus 3 is 57.
Let us check by going backwards. 57 take away 3 brings us back to 54.
So when you add a small number and there is room in the ones, keep the tens and just add the ones.
Let us multiply 9 by 11. Look at the sign first. It is times, so we multiply.
11 is easier in two pieces. Split it into 10 and 1.
First the tens piece. What is 9 times 10?

ask.ifNot: 9 tens is 90. Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left.

beats.say: 9 times 10 is 90. That is the tens piece done.
Now the ones piece. 9 times 1 is 9.
Add the two pieces. 90 and 9 make 99.
So 9 times 11 is 99.
The plan: break the big number up, multiply each piece, and add the pieces.
Let us take 30 away from 42. The sign is a minus, so we are taking away, not adding.
30 is a round number, full tens and no ones. So split the 42 into 40 and 2.
Take the tens away first. What is 40 take away 30?

ask.ifNot: 4 tens take away 3 tens leaves 1 ten. And 1 ten is 10.

beats.say: 4 tens take away 3 tens leaves 1 ten. That is 10.
The 2 ones were never touched, so put them back. 10 and 2 make 12.
So 42 minus 30 is 12.
Check by adding back. 12 plus 30 makes 42, the number we started with.
So when you take away a round number, only the tens change. The ones stay as they are.
Look at the signs here. A minus, then a times, then a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 3 times 7.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 3 times 7. It goes first.
3 times 7 is 21. Write 21 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Just a minus and a plus now. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 41 take away 21.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 41 take away 21 is 20.
And now the plus. 20 plus 12 is 32.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a minus, a times and a plus.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 7 times 2.

beats.say: Times is the boss here. It goes before plus and minus, so put a box round 7 times 2.
7 times 2 is 14. Write 14 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Just a minus and a plus now. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 16 take away 14.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 16 take away 14 is 2.
And now the plus. 2 plus 1 is 3.
The trap in this sum is the minus at the front. It looks like the place to start, but the times must go first.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is our sum: a minus, a times and a plus. The order we do them in changes the answer, so let us get it right.
Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So 3 times 8 goes first.

beats.say: Times goes first. Box 3 times 8.
3 times 8 is 24. Write 24 where the box was, and copy the rest.
Now left to right. 50 take away 24. Take away 20 to get 30, then 4 more to get 26.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: Look back at the sum. There is still a plus 2 at the end, waiting for its turn.

beats.say: 26 plus 2 is 28.
The big trap is doing 50 take away 3 first, because it is on the left. Times always jumps ahead of plus and minus.
So: times first, then plus and minus from left to right, all the way to the end.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a minus, a times and a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 7 times 3.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 7 times 3. It goes first.
7 times 3 is 21. Write 21 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 29 take away 21.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 29 take away 21 is 8.
And now the plus. 8 plus 8 is 16.
The trap in this sum is the minus at the front. It looks like the place to start, but the times must go first.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is a sum with a bracket. A bracket is like a little box that says: open me first.
So what do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: The bracket goes first. Inside the bracket is 15 plus 5.

beats.say: Bracket first. 15 plus 5 is 20.
Now the bracket has turned into 20. The sum is 20 times 3.
2 times 3 is 6, so 20 times 3 is 60.
Careful: without the bracket, we would do 5 times 3 first and get a different answer. The bracket tells us to add first.
So: brackets first, then the rest.
Here is our sum. It has a divide and a plus in it.
Which job goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide goes before plus. So 36 divided by 6 comes first.

beats.say: Divide goes before plus. So box 36 divided by 6.
